raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the prototype angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), combining valsartan-mediated blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor with sacubitril, a prodrug whose active metabolite inhibits neprilysin. The therapeutic premise is biologically coherent: suppress maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system signaling while augmenting endogenous natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and related vasoactive peptides that promote natriuresis, vasodilation, and antifibrotic signaling. Early pharmacologic studies showed sustained neprilysin inhibition and blood pressure lowering with LCZ696, with tolerability supporting larger heart failure trials [1], [2].

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) came from PARADIGM-HF, a large randomized comparison of sacubitril/valsartan 200 mg twice daily versus enalapril 10 mg twice daily in ambulatory symptomatic patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%, later amended to ≤35% [3]. The trial was stopped early because sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, as well as all-cause mortality [4]. Subsequent analyses reinforced that benefit was clinically broad: sacubitril/valsartan reduced clinical progression among survivors [5], retained efficacy and acceptable tolerability across age groups [6], and provided consistent absolute benefit across baseline-risk strata [7]. Importantly, patients unable to maintain target doses still appeared to derive relative benefit compared with lower-dose enalapril [8].

Safety and ancillary effects have shaped clinical use. Compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan caused more symptomatic hypotension but less cough, less creatinine elevation, and less hyperkalemia in the main trial [4]. Among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, severe hyperkalemia was less frequent with sacubitril/valsartan than with enalapril [9]. In patients with diabetes, treatment was associated with lower HbA1c and fewer initiations of insulin or oral glucose-lowering therapy, an observation that remains hypothesis-generating but clinically relevant [10]. Renal analyses suggested slower decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate and fewer serious renal events despite modest albuminuria increases, supporting use with careful monitoring rather than avoidance in stable chronic kidney disease [11]. Interpretation of natriuretic peptides requires nuance: BNP may rise because it is a neprilysin substrate, whereas NT-proBNP remains useful for diagnosis, prognosis, and response assessment [12].

Patient-centered outcomes also favor ARNI therapy. PARADIGM-HF showed modest but significant attenuation of deterioration in health-related quality of life [13], and secondary analyses suggested benefit in physical and social activity limitations [14]. Practical initiation was addressed by TITRATION, which showed that gradual uptitration improved tolerability, especially in patients naïve to high-dose renin–angiotensin system blockade [15]. In acute decompensated heart failure, PIONEER-HF demonstrated that in-hospital initiation after hemodynamic stabilization produced greater NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, or angioedema [16]. Biomarker analyses showed early reductions in myocardial injury and wall-stress markers [17], and TRANSITION supported feasibility of starting before discharge or shortly after discharge [18]. Reverse-remodeling studies complement these findings: EVALUATE-HF did not significantly improve aortic stiffness but showed favorable cardiac structural signals [19], while PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reduction after initiation with improvements in LVEF and ventricular volumes [20]. A randomized study in functional mitral regurgitation suggested sacubitril/valsartan may reduce regurgitant severity beyond valsartan alone, plausibly through ventricular remodeling and afterload effects [21].

Evidence in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is more complex. PARAMOUNT showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and left atrial reverse remodeling signals versus valsartan in HFpEF [22], prompting PARAGON-HF [23]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested benefit in patients with LVEF below the median and in women [24], [25]. A pooled analysis across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF supported a continuum of benefit, greatest below normal LVEF and attenuating as EF rises [26]. Renal outcomes in PARAGON-HF were favorable, with slower eGFR decline and fewer renal events [27]. Thus, ARNI therapy is established in HFrEF and increasingly considered in mildly reduced or “lower-range preserved” EF, while routine use in high-EF HFpEF remains individualized.

Beyond chronic HF, PARADISE-MI tested sacubitril/valsartan after acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced LVEF, pulmonary congestion, or both. It did not significantly reduce the primary composite versus ramipril, so post-MI ACE-inhibitor/ARB standards remain largely intact, though exploratory signals continue to inform risk-based research [28]. Current American and European guidelines recommend sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic HFrEF, either replacing ACE inhibitor/ARB in eligible patients or used de novo when feasible, with attention to blood pressure, renal function, potassium, cost, and the mandatory washout after ACE-inhibitor exposure to reduce angioedema risk [29], [30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major advance in HFrEF: it improves survival, reduces hospitalization, supports remodeling, and can be initiated safely across inpatient and outpatient settings when patients are appropriately selected and monitored.
